Wow, paragraph 2:

Brutal honesty.

"ain't no", that tells you how intelligent this idiot is.

They have the potential to be zero emission with electric generation from solar, wind, geothermal, etc - the cars themselves do not emit anything, and power plants at scale are FAR more efficient than internal combustion engines.

The article goes on to mention that at scale, power plants are more efficient than internal combustion engines, but there's still a non-zero carbon emission no matter what is generating the power.

There's a thing in mathematics called a limit, which is "the value that a function or sequence 'approaches' as the input or index approaches some value." The minimum limit for carbon emissions is theoretically zero, but we have yet to reach that in any aspect of life. When he says "There ain't no such thing as zero emission battery cars", he is speaking an as-of-yet universal law. A "zero emission battery car" is literally impossible with current technology, and may never actually be achieved. There will always be a carbon footprint somewhere in the lifetime of the vehicle, whether it's in the manufacturing process or after the vehicle has been made.

Once a wind turbine, or a solar panel, etc is produced - it effectively uses no more energy during its lifetime. And it will produce many megawatts of energy. It is effectively 0, because the ratio of energy these systems create are so large in number that the energy used to create them in the first place is negligible. Now, we can get into semantics and argue that "nothing is ever TRUELY zero"...but then you're missing the entire fucking point.

Assuming it's placed in the right spot to actually produce enough energy to offset whatever went into creating it.

Nuclear energy, on the other hand, does produce a net benefit to the environment. Not only does it generate far more than energy than current renewables can produce over the course of their respective lifetimes, but it doesn't matter where you put it - it will always generate power, whether it's sunny, rainy, dry, cold, breezy, etc. The only problem here in the U.S. is that we can't build Breeder reactors. That would solve most of our nuclear waste issues.

Nuclear is not an option because every time an accident happens, we're literally making part of the world uninhabitable forever. We've proven that governments, and bureaucrats cannot handle these things properly. How long is the longest that a nuclear reactor has lasted? 40-50 years? And then something goes wrong and makes that place uninhabitable for the next 100,000,000? No. Solar, Wind, Geothermal - the technologies are simple, non-harmful, easy to produce, and if something goes wrong people don't die en-masse.

According to Wikipedia, the oldest operational nuclear power plant is that has not been decommissioned is Beznau Unit 1 in Switzerland. It went operational in 1969 and is planned to operate until 2029, a total of 60 years, assuming nothing happens to it. It produces a net 265 MW of power.

An interesting quote from the section on Swiss Nuclear Power Plants:

As of 8 December 2014, the Swiss parliament has voted to limit the operational life-time of Beznau I & II to no more than 60 years, and to enshrine a ban of constructing new reactors in the Constitution. In addition, an Initiative of limiting the life-span of all nuclear reactors to 45 years will have to be voted upon the Swiss, irrespective of whether the legislature will actually enforce the constitutional amendment or not.

Additionally, according to the Nuclear Energy Institute, there are currently 449 operational Nuclear Power Plants in 30 countries worldwide.
